column2: When men keep this auspicious Naga vow thus, O best of brahmins, poisons soon perish and serpents do not bite.
From the fourth of the bright half of Margashirsha, for a year, O lord of sages, one should keep one meal a day; the second year eat only at night;
the third year eat only unasked food, and the fourth fast. In this order a man keeps it duly for four years;
then, completing it, at its end the great vow-keeper, having taken the concluding bath, should have made a golden mouse-chariot for the lord of the earth's hosts,
or, if unable, a white lotus with fine petals drawn with colours; placing a pitcher on it with a copper vessel,
he should fill it with white rice, and on it place the lord of the Ganas covered with a pair of cloths and worship him with perfumes and the like,
offering modakas as food, saying, "May Ganesha be pleased," and keep vigil with songs, music, Puranic stories and the like.
At clear dawn, having bathed, he should perform the oblation according to rule, with sesame, rice, barley, white mustard and ghee with sugar pieces,
with the sixteen names: Gana, Ganadhipa, Kushmanda, Tripurantaka, Lambodara, Ekadanta, Rukmadamshtra, Vighnapa,
Brahma, Yama, Varuna, Soma, Surya, Hutashana, Gandhamadi and Parameshthi —
each beginning with the pranava and ending in the dative with 'namah,' offered in the fire; and with 'vakratundaya' in the dative ending with the armour syllable, a hundred and eight times.
Then offering with the vyahritis according to one's power, one should make the full oblation, worship the guardians of the directions, and then feed brahmins,
twenty-four of them, with modakas and milk-rice; then give a cow with its calf and a fee to the teacher,
and to others too according to one's means, and then a large gift; bowing, circumambulating and dismissing the best of brahmins,
one should eat with one's kin, glad at heart. A man who keeps this vow enjoys the finest pleasures here
and gains union with Vishnu by Ganesha's grace. Some call this the Vara vow, O Narada;
its procedure is the same, and its fruit here is equal. On the fourth of the month of Pausha, praying devoutly to Vighnesha,
one should feed a single brahmin with modakas and give a fee; when this is done, O sage, the vow-keeper becomes a vessel of prosperity.
On the fourth of the dark half of Magha the Sankashta vow is declared: making the resolve to fast, the vow-keeper, with discipline,
should remain restrained until moonrise; then, when the moon has risen, making an earthen image of the lord of the Ganas,
he should place it on a seat with its weapons and mount, and duly worship it with the sixteen offerings,
offering modakas and sesame sweets with jaggery; then an arghya in a copper vessel mixed with red sandal,
with kusha, durva, flowers, unbroken rice, shami leaves and curd, should be prepared and offered to the moon:
O Moon, jewel of the ocean of the sky, lord of Daksha's daughters, image of Ganesha, accept the arghya given by me.
Having given this divine, sin-destroying arghya to Ganesha, and fed the best brahmins according to his means, he should eat himself with their leave.
Having kept thus the auspicious vow called Sankashta, O brahmin, one becomes rich in wealth and grain and does not meet with distress.
On the fourth of the bright half of Magha is the unsurpassed Gauri vow; on it Gauri is to be worshipped together with the hosts of yoginis,
by men and especially women, with kunda flowers and saffron, with red thread, red flowers and lac,
with incense, lamps and offerings, with jaggery and ginger, milk, milk-rice, salt and spinach;
women whose husbands live and fine brahmins are to be honoured; gifts should be given for the increase of good fortune, and one should eat with one's kin.
This Gauri vow, O brahmin, increases good fortune and health; it should be kept every year by women and men alike.
Others call it the Dhundhi vow, some the Kunda vow, others the Lalita vow, and others the Shanti vow.
Bathing, giving, japa, oblation — all done on this day, O sage, becomes a thousandfold by the grace of the tusked one.
On the fourth in the month of Phalguna is the auspicious Dhundhiraja vow; a man should feed brahmins with sesame cakes and eat them himself.
Devoted to the worship of Ganesha, with gifts, oblations and worship made with sesame alone, one gains success by his grace.
Making a golden elephant-faced image and worshipping it carefully, one should give it to an excellent brahmin for the increase of all prosperity.
In whatever month the fourth falls on a Sunday or a Tuesday, O best of brahmins, it gives special fruit.
On all fourth days, bright and dark, Vighnesha alone, lord of gods, should be worshipped by those intent on devotion.
worshipping with gold, silver and the like, curd, unbroken rice, kusha and water, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps and heaps of food offerings,
then circumambulating that wealth and bowing to it, praying with devotion, one should give it to the best of brahmins:
This gold, silver and other wealth given to brahmins — may it bear endless fruit for me in birth after birth.
For one who gives wealth thus with devotion, O Narada, the lord of wealth is pleased and grants prosperity in gold and the like.
A man who keeps this vow, feeding brahmins with devotion, should then eat himself, surrounded by wife, children and friends.
On the fifth of the dark half of Bhadra one should satisfy the Nagas with milk;
for seven generations his family is free from fear of serpents. On the fifth of the bright half of Bhadra one should worship the best of sages:
bathing in the morning in a river or the like and diligently performing the daily rites, coming home, one should carefully make an altar of earth,
smear it with cow dung and adorn it with flowers; spreading kusha grass there, one should worship the seven brahmin sages
with perfumes, various flowers, incense and fine lamps: Kashyapa, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra, Gautama,
Jamadagni and Vasishtha — these seven are remembered as the sages. Preparing an arghya duly and giving it to them,
the wise one should cook a food offering with shyamaka and other uncultivated grains; offering it and dismissing them, one should eat the same oneself.
Keeping it by this procedure every year for seven years, at the end of the vow one should choose seven Vedic teachers,
and have seven images made of gold according to one's means, with matted locks, rosaries and water-pots;
placing them in pitchers of copper or clay, one should bathe them duly with devotion, each with the five nectars,
then worship them with the sixteen offerings, give the arghya, and then perform an oblation with sesame, rice, barley and the like,
with the verse 'Sahastoma' or with the name-mantras separately, and with other holy mantras, and make the full oblation.
Then one should give seven cows with clothes and ornaments, and honour the teacher with clothes, ornaments and adornments;
then with the teacher's leave give the images to the brahmins, feed them with devotion, bow and dismiss them.
Then, sitting with loved ones, one should eat the food of six flavours left by the brahmins and rejoice with one's kin.
Having kept this vow of the Ganga and enjoyed desired pleasures, by the grace of the seven sages one rides in an excellent celestial car.
On the fifth of the bright half of Ashvina is the Upangalalita vow;
making a golden image of her according to one's means, O Narada, one should worship it duly with the sixteen offerings;
cooked food with fruits and ghee, with a fee, should be given to an excellent brahmin for the completion of the vow:
Boon-giving one, with your mount and your power, you have been worshipped by me; Mother, show me grace and go to your own abode.
On the fifth of the bright half of Kartika the unsurpassed Jaya vow should be kept with faith for the destruction of sins, O best of brahmins.
Worshipping Jaya duly with concentration and the sixteen offerings, O brahmin, then, pure and adorned,
one should feed a single brahmin, give him a fee, dismiss him and then eat in silence.
Whoever, filled with devotion, bathes on Jaya's day — his sins perish like deer attacked by a lion.
The fruit declared for bathing at the end of the horse-sacrifice is obtained, O brahmin, even by bathing on Jaya's day.
The sonless obtains a son, the barren woman conceives, the sick is freed from disease and the bound from bondage.
On the fifth of the bright half of Margashirsha, worshipping the Nagas duly, one gains freedom from fear of serpents and rejoices with one's kin.
On the fifth of the bright half of Pausha, worshipping Madhusudana, one obtains the desires one wishes; there is no doubt.
On the fifth of every month, bright and dark, O Narada, the worship of the ancestors and of the Nagas is always commended.
Standing before her, one should pray to that Goddess, beloved of Girisha: "At Gangadvara, Kushavarta, Bilvaka and the Blue Mountain,
having bathed at Kanakhala, O Goddess, you gained Hara as your husband; O Lalita, fortunate Goddess, giver of happiness and good fortune,
grant me endless good fortune; salutations to you." With this mantra, and with lovely champaka flowers,
worshipping her duly, one should place food offerings before her; with cucumbers, pumpkins, coconuts, fine pomegranates,
citrons, tundiras, bitter gourds and chirbhatas — fruits of the season — one should make a display before her,
with sprouted grain, rows of fine lamps, incense with ... and sohalaka and karanjaka cakes,
jaggery flowers, karnaveshtas, modakas and small sweets — many kinds of food offerings according to one's means.
Having worshipped thus duly, at night there should be a festival of vigil with songs, music, actors and dances, and many sprinklings;
the virtuous woman with her friends should spend that night vigorously, and should not close her eyes for the four watches;
by closing her eyes she would become unfortunate, sinful and barren. Having kept vigil thus, on the seventh she should take [the image] to a river,
worship it with perfumes and flowers, with songs and music leading, and give the food offerings and the like to an excellent brahmin, O best of brahmins.
Having bathed and returned home, then offering to Vaishvanara, worshipping gods, ancestors and men, married women
and maidens, and feeding fifteen brahmins with many kinds of food, and giving abundant gifts,
saying, "May Lalita be well pleased with me," she should dismiss them. Whoever keeps this supreme vow that gives good fortune,
man or woman, hear the fruit of their merit: whatever is gained by vows, austerities, gifts or disciplines
is gained here by this — what need of more words, O Narada? After death, reaching the eternal world of Shiva,
one rejoices long with the Goddess Lalita as a friend in Shiva's world. The sixth of the bright half in the month of Nabhasya is called Chandana;
worshipping the Goddess on it one gains her world. When it is joined with Rohini, Pata and Tuesday, it becomes Kapila;
worshipping the Sun on it, the vow-keeper intent on discipline gains the desires he wishes by the Sun's grace.
Giving food, japa, oblation, libations to ancestors, gods and sages — all done then is to be known as imperishable, O best of divine sages.
Worshipping a tawny cow with clothes, garlands and unguents, one should give it to a knower of the Veda for the pleasure of the twelve-souled Sun.
Then on the sixth of the bright half of Isha, Katyayani is to be worshipped, O brahmin, with perfumes and auspicious articles and various food offerings;
then asking forgiveness of the queen of gods and bowing, one should dismiss her; a sand image is to be worshipped here, or a virtuous brahmin woman, joyfully,
with fine clothes and ornaments, for Katyayani's pleasure. A maiden gains a husband, and a woman the son she desires,
by Katyayani's grace; there is no doubt. On the sixth of the bright half of Kartika, the great-souled Six-faced one
obtained the fortunate Devasena, given by all the gods; so on that day, worshipping Devasena, best of goddesses, and the Six-faced one
with all charming offerings, one gains incomparable success as the heart desires, O best of brahmins.
Here too one should properly perform the worship of Fire that is prescribed, with oblations of various substances, preceded by fire-worship.
On the sixth of the bright half of Margashirsha the asura Taraka was slain, and Skanda received honour arranged by Brahma and others;
so on this day one should worship Skanda with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, fruits, clothes, ornaments and various food offerings.
If it is joined with Sunday and with Shatabhisha, it is declared as the one called Champa, O best of sages;
on it the god Vishveshvara, destroyer of sins, should be seen, worshipped, known and remembered by one who desires happiness;
bathing, giving and all else here are said to be imperishable. On the sixth of the bright half of the month of Pausha, O brahmin, the lord of the day,
in Vishnu's form, protector of the world, the eternal one, appeared;
so he should be worshipped on this day with substances headed by perfumes, with food offerings, clothes, ornaments and the like, by those who desire all happiness.
The bright sixth in the month of Magha is remembered as the one called Varuna; on it one should worship Varuna, the eternal, in Vishnu's form,
with red perfumes, cloths and flowers, food offerings, incense and lamps; having worshipped thus duly, whatever a man desires,
he obtains as fruit and rejoices by his grace. On the sixth of the bright half of Phalguna, O brahmin, the god Pashupati,
making him of clay according to rule, one should worship with offerings; bathing him with the Shatarudra, separately with the five nectars and water,
anointing him with perfumes, with very white unbroken rice, white flowers, bilva leaves, datura flowers and fruits,
worshipping him with various food offerings and waving lights duly, asking forgiveness and bowing, one should dismiss him to Kailasa.
Man or woman who worships Shiva thus, O sage, enjoys excellent pleasures here and at the end attains Shiva's goal.
Covering it with a pair of cloths, one should worship with perfumes, incense and the like: "Salutations to you, lotus-handed one; salutations to you, bearer of the universe;
O maker of day, salutations to you; O maker of light, salutations to you." Having prayed thus to the Lord of gods, when the sun has set,
one should give that lotus with a pitcher of water and a tawny cow to a brahmin; on that day one should fast and eat on the next day;
feeding brahmins with devotion one gains the completion of the vow. Here too is the Nimba vow; hear its procedure from me:
worship of the Sun is remembered with neem leaves, O best of brahmins, with the mantra 'Khakholkaya' beginning with the pranava, O Narada;
then one should eat a neem leaf and sleep on the ground in silence; on the next day, feeding brahmins, one should eat with one's kin.
This neem-leaf vow gives all happiness to those who keep it. This seventh day is declared as the one called Sharkara; hear of that too:
as the Sun drank nectar, drops of nectar fell from his hand to the earth and became rice, mung, barley and sugarcane,
and from that came sugar, like nectar, the essence of sugarcane; it is dear to the Sun, and therefore sugar is holy for offerings to gods and ancestors.
The Sharkara Saptami gives the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, quells all sorrow and increases offspring.
On it the gift of sugar and eating sugar should be done with care; this vow is dear to the Sun.
Whoever keeps it with supreme devotion attains a good goal. On the seventh of the bright half of Jyeshtha, the Sun himself was born as Indra;
worshipping him duly, fasting and with senses controlled, one attains heaven, O brahmin, by the grace of the king of gods.
On the seventh of the bright half of Ashadha the Sun named Vivasvan was born; worshipping him there separately with perfumes, flowers and the like,
one gains union with the Sun, O best of brahmins, without doubt. On the seventh of the bright half of Shravana is the auspicious vow called Avyanga:
a cotton cloth of four and a half cubits should be given to the lord of rays at the end of worship for his pleasure; this vow brings good.
If it is joined with Hasta, it destroys sin; giving, japa and oblation on it all become imperishable.
On the seventh of the bright half of Bhadra is the Amuktabharana vow; the worship of Mahesha with Uma is declared here,
worshipping with the sixteen offerings beginning with Ganga water; praying and bowing, one should dismiss him for the fulfilment of all desires.
This is also the Phala Saptami; its procedure is told: coconut, brinjal, orange, citron,
pumpkin, brihati and areca — these seven fruits one should place before Mahadeva, and another thread,
made of seven strands with seven knots, O best of brahmins; worshipping it with supreme devotion, one should wear it on the left hand
if a woman, on the right if a man, until the year is complete; feeding seven brahmins with milk-rice and dismissing them,
the wise one should eat himself for the completion of the vow, and those fruits should be given to the seven brahmins.
Having kept it thus duly for seven years, the vow-keeper gains union with Mahadeva, O brahmin.
In the bright half of Ashvina is to be known the Shubha Saptami: on it, having bathed and worshipped and had the best brahmins recite blessings,
beginning with a tawny cow, worshipping her, one should then pray: "I give you, auspicious one; may Aryaman himself be pleased.
Protect the whole world, since you are born of dharma." Saying this, having given her to a knower of the Veda with a fee,
and bowing, one should dismiss them and oneself taste the five cow products; having kept the vow thus, the next day, feeding the best brahmins,
one should eat the food left by the brahmins. Done with faith, this is well spoken of, O brahmin;
by the grace of the God of gods one gains enjoyment and liberation. Then on the bright seventh of Kartika is the vow called Shaka:
on it one should give seven vegetables with golden lotuses to seven brahmins, and then live on vegetables oneself;
on the second day, feeding brahmins and giving them a fee of food, dismissing them, one should eat in silence with one's kin.
On the bright seventh of Margashirsha the Mitra vow is declared: what was Vishnu's right eye became here
the Sun named Mitra, born of Aditi from Kashyapa; so on this day, O brahmin, worshipping him by the procedure described,
feeding seven brahmins with sweet food and the like, and giving a fee of gold, one should dismiss them and eat oneself.
Keeping this duly, one surely goes to the Sun's world; a brahmin gains Brahma's world, and a shudra birth in a good family.
On the bright seventh of Pausha is the vow called Abhaya: fasting, worshipping the Sun at the three junctions of the day and sleeping on the ground,
one should give a brahmin a prastha of modakas made with food soaked in milk, and feed seven or eight others, giving a fee
of land or gold, and dismissing them, eat oneself. This vow called Abhaya is held to give fearlessness to all.
Other brahmins call this the Martanda vow; the wise declare them one, since the deity is one.
On the dark seventh of Magha is the vow called Sarvapti: fasting on that day, worshipping a golden image of the Sun's disc
with perfumes, flowers and the like, and keeping vigil at night, on the next day feeding seven brahmins with milk-rice,
giving them coconuts as fees, and then giving the teacher the golden disc of the Sun with another fee,
praying earnestly and dismissing them, one should then eat. This is declared the Sarvaptida, granting all desires;
by the power of this vow ... is accomplished in every way. On the bright seventh of Magha is remembered the vow called Achala;
it is the birth-anniversary of the three-eyed one and removes all sins; it is also the Ratha Saptami, which grants universal sovereignty.

On it, worshipping a golden image of the Sun on a chariot with golden horses, one should give it with an elephant; whoever does so with feeling and devotion goes to Shambhu's world and rejoices, having enjoyed pleasures here too.
This is also the Bhaskari Saptami, like a crore of shining planets; a bath at dawn on it is prescribed.
Placing seven leaves each of arka and jujube on the head, one should bathe to quell the sins of seven births.
Here the Lord Aditya himself declared the son-giving vow: "Whoever worships me duly on the bright seventh of Magha,
greatly pleased, I will become his son with my own portion." So, with senses controlled, fasting day and night,
one should worship, and on the next day perform an oblation and then feed brahmins with curd-rice, milk and milk-rice.
Whoever keeps the Putra Saptami by this procedure obtains a good son, long-lived and healthy.
On the bright seventh of Tapasya one should keep the Arkaputa vow: worship the Sun with arka leaves and eat arka leaves,
and constantly recite the Sun's name — this is the Arkaputa vow; it gives wealth and sons and destroys all sins.
Some call this the Trivargada vow, O brahmin; others the Yajna vow, with oblation duly performed.
On all the seventh days in all months, O best of brahmins, the worship of the Sun is declared to grant all desires; enough.
The Durva Ashtami vow is declared here; hear it from me. On durva grass grown in a clean place, O best of brahmins,
placing a linga, one should worship with devotion with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, curd, unbroken rice, fruits and the like,
and at the end of worship give an arghya with two mantras, with full concentration: "O Durva, you are born of nectar, saluted by gods and asuras;
grant good fortune and offspring; be the accomplisher of all tasks. As you spread over the earth with branches and sub-branches,
so grant me widespread offspring, unageing and immortal." Then circumambulating and feeding brahmins there,
eating oneself, one should go home, having given the brahmins a fee, and excellent, sweet and fragrant fruits.
Thus the Durva Ashtami is holy and removes men's sins, O brahmin, for all four classes and especially for women.
The woman who out of delusion does not worship durva duly suffers widowhood for three births; there is no doubt.
When the eighth falls with the constellation Jyeshtha, O brahmin, it is to be known as the one named Jyeshtha; worshipped, it destroys sin.
Beginning from this day is the sixteen-day vow declared for Mahalakshmi, increasing all prosperity:
I shall keep your Mahalakshmi vow, devoted to you; may it reach completion without obstacle by your grace.
Saying this, one should tie a thread on the right hand with sixteen knots and sixteen strands,
and then the vow-keeper should worship Mahalakshmi daily with perfumes and the like until the dark eighth, when the wise should perform the concluding rite:
making a cloth pavilion over a sarvatobhadra mandala, installing a pitcher well and lighting a lamp,
taking the thread off the arm and placing it below the pitcher, making four golden images of her form,
one should have them bathed with water and the five nectars and duly worship them with the sixteen offerings.
A vigil should be kept there with the sound of songs and instruments; then, when midnight comes and the nectar-rayed moon has risen,
giving an arghya with sandal and other substances duly, one should offer it to Mahalakshmi dwelling in the moon's orb:

O brother of Mahalakshmi, born of the ocean of milk, abode of nectar, with Rohini accept my arghya.
naradapuran:116:64	O Kamala, born of the ocean of milk, dwelling in the lotus, dwelling on Vishnu's breast, grant me all desires.
naradapuran:116:65	O sole lord, lord of the world, beloved of Jamadagni, imperishable Renuka, protect me, Goddess; mother of Rama, bring me good.
Having prayed to Mahalakshmi with these mantras, one should properly honour the wives of Vedic scholars with perfumes, lac and collyrium,
feed them, and offer into the fire bilva, lotuses and milk-rice, or failing these, ghee, O brahmin, and fuel sticks and sesame from homes,
and then to Mrityunjaya for the quelling of all diseases. Sandal, palm leaf, a flower garland and unbroken rice,
durva, safflower thread, a pair [of cloths] or a bilva fruit, and foods — sixteen of each item — in a new winnowing basket,
covered with another basket, the vow-keeper should give with the mantra: "Lakshmi, born of the ocean of milk, sister of the moon,
beloved of Vishnu, be pleased by this vow." And those four images should be given to Vedic scholars;
then, feeding four brahmins and sixteen married women with sweet food, one should dismiss them with fees.
Then, with the rules completed, one should eat with loved ones. Having kept this vow of Mahalakshmi duly, O brahmin,
enjoying desired pleasures of this world, one dwells long in Lakshmi's world. This is also declared the Ashoka Ashtami, on which Rama's vow is completed;
here the worship of the ashoka is prescribed, and one meal is remembered. A woman who keeps the Ashoka vow becomes free from sorrow in every birth,
wherever she is born; there is no doubt. In the bright half of Ashvina, O brahmin, is declared the Mahashtami;
on it the worship of Durga with all offerings is declared; observing a fast or one meal on the Mahashtami,
one obtains glory on every side and rejoices long like a god. On the eighth of the dark half of Urja the vow called Karaka is remembered;
on it Shambhu with Uma should be worshipped with care, and the vow-keepers should always give an arghya at moonrise,
desiring a son endowed with all virtues and various happiness. On the bright half of Kartika is declared the Gopashtami;
on it one should worship cows, give them mouthfuls, circumambulate them, follow them and give gifts, desiring all prosperity.
On the dark eighth of Margashirsha, a couple made of darbha, Anagha and Anagha, with many sons,
placed in a fine spot smeared with cow dung, should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers and various offerings;
feeding a brahmin couple, one should dismiss them with a fee. A man or woman who keeps this vow duly
obtains a son endowed with good marks; there is no doubt.
On the bright eighth of Margashirsha, fasting and keeping vigil in the presence of Kalabhairava, one is freed from great sins;
whatever evil deed has been done in human birth is all dissolved by the sight of Kalabhairava.
Then on the bright eighth of Pausha is the shraddha called Ashtaka, which satisfies the ancestors for a year and increases the family line.
On the bright eighth of Pausha, worshipping Shiva with devotion, practising devotion alone, one gains enjoyment and liberation.
On the dark eighth of Magha one should devoutly worship Bhadrakali, destroyer of hosts of enemies and giver of all desires.
On the bright eighth of the month of Magha one should offer libations to Bhishma, O brahmin, desiring unbroken offspring and invincibility.
On the dark eighth of Phalguna one should worship the goddess Bhima; there, devoted to the vow, O brahmin, for the fulfilment of all desires.
On the bright eighth of Phalguna, worshipping Shiva and Shiva's consort properly with perfumes and the like, one becomes lord of all siddhis.
In the latter half of Phalguna, on the eighth, one should worship Shitala with all kinds of cooked food duly prepared on the seventh:

Shitala, you are the mother of the world; Shitala, you are the father of the world; Shitala, you are the upholder of the world; salutations again and again to Shitala.
naradapuran:116:96	I salute the goddess Shitala, seated on a donkey, naked, with broom and pitcher, destroyer of pustular disease.
For those who, standing in water, recite "Shitala, Shitala" thus, the goddess Shitala quells pustular disease.
Whoever worships Shitala with these mantras, O brahmin, has peace for a year by Shitala's grace.
On the eighth of both fortnights in every month, worshipping Shiva or Shiva's consort duly, one obtains the fruit one desires.
The best of brahmins [Chandika] was consecrated to sovereignty over all; so one should worship her here, fasting and with senses controlled.
Whoever worships Chandika duly on the ninth of both fortnights of Radha rejoices with the gods in a celestial car.
On the bright ninth of Jyeshtha the best of men, fasting, should duly worship Uma and feed maidens and brahmins,
give fees according to his devotion, and eat rice with milk. Whoever keeps this Uma vow duly, O brahmin,
enjoys excellent pleasures here and at the end attains heaven. In the month of Ashadha, O best of brahmins, whoever in both fortnights
eats at night and worships the white Aindri seated on Airavata becomes an enjoyer of pleasures in the world of the gods, travelling by the path of the gods.
In the month of Shravana, O best of brahmins, whoever eats at night or fasts in both fortnights and worships Kaumari Chandika,
the remover of sins, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, various food offerings and feeding of maidens —
whoever keeps this excellent Kaumari vow with devotion goes in a celestial car to the eternal world of the Goddess.
The bright ninth in Bhadra is declared as the one called Nanda; whoever duly worships Durga on it with offerings
obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice and is honoured in Vishnu's world. The bright ninth of Ashvina is declared as the Mahanavami;
on it, in the afternoon, the worship of the shami should be performed toward the east, O brahmin; then at night, in the first watch, sword, bow, arrows, mace,
trident, spear, axe, dagger, shield, buckler, umbrella, banner, elephant, horse, cow and bull, book, scales,
staff, noose, discus and conch — worshipping these with perfumes and other offerings, one should sacrifice a buffalo there to Bhadrakali.
Having made the offering thus and eaten cooked food, and given fees to brahmins, one should complete the vow there.
Whoever thus worships Durga, destroyer of men's misfortunes, enjoys excellent pleasures here and at the end attains heaven.
The bright ninth of Kartika is declared as the Akshaya; on it one should properly offer libations at the foot of the ashvattha
to the gods, sages and ancestors, O Narada, and with the mantras of one's own Vedic branch give an arghya to the Sun;
then feeding brahmins with sweet food, O lord of sages, and eating oneself, one should go about freely, having given the brahmins fees.
For whoever does this with devotion, japa, giving, worship of brahmins and oblation all become imperishable — such is the word of the ordinance.
The bright ninth of Margashirsha is declared as the Nandini; whoever, fasting on it, worships the Mother of the world
with perfumes and the like shares in the fruit of the horse-sacrifice; there is no doubt. On the bright ninth of Pausha one should worship Mahamaya,
keeping one meal, O brahmin, to gain the fruit of the Vajapeya. The bright ninth in the month of Magha is worshipped by the world;
it is called Mahananda, ever bringing men bliss; bathing, giving, japa, oblation and fasting on it
all become imperishable; there is no doubt. The ninth of the bright half of Phalguna, O best of brahmins,
is Ananda, most holy, remembered as removing all sins; whoever, fasting, worships Ananda on it, O best of brahmins,
obtains the desires he wishes — truly, truly, I declare it.

having fasted or eaten once, at midnight one should offer bali with cakes and the like in the ten directions, at home or outside the town,
in an eight-petalled mandala drawn on ground smeared with cow dung, with these mantras, O best of brahmins, having worshipped Ganesha and the others:

Whatever sin of mine lies in the east, done here by sinful deed, may Indra, king of the gods, granter of all wishes, destroy it today.

Having thus offered bali in the ten directions with concentration, one should, untiring, cast a bali outside for Kshetrapala.
Having performed the rite thus, the wise one should spend the rest of the night with auspicious songs, recitations of hymns, japa and the like;
in the morning, having bathed and worshipped the guardians of the world and twelve excellent brahmins, feeding them, one should give fees according to one's means.
Having kept this vow thus, O brahmin, and enjoyed auspicious pleasures of this world, and the happiness of heaven for an age, one becomes a universal king.
On the bright tenth of Margashirsha one should keep the Arogya vow: worship ten brahmins with perfumes and the like, drink the water of their feet,
give fees, dismiss them and eat one meal. Having kept this vow, O brahmin, one gains health on earth,
and by Dharmaraja's grace rejoices in heaven like a god. On the bright tenth of Pausha one should worship the Vishvedevas:
Kratu, Daksha, Vasu, Satya, Kala, Kama, Muni, Guru, Vipra and Rama — in these ten Keshava abides;
placing them on seats of darbha, one should worship them with perfumes, incense, lamps and food offerings, O Narada,
give a fee to each, bow and dismiss them, and give those fees to excellent brahmins or to the teacher.
Having performed the rite thus and eating once, the vow-keeper becomes an enjoyer of both worlds, O brahmin sage; there is no doubt.
On the bright tenth of Magha, fasting and with senses controlled, one should properly worship the ten gods called Angirasas,
making them of gold, O brahmin, with perfumes and other offerings: Atma, Ayu, Manas, Daksha, Mada, Prana,
Barhishman, Gavishtha, Datta and Satya — these are the ten. Feeding ten brahmins with sweet food, O Narada,
one should give them the images in order to attain the world of heaven. On the bright tenth of the last month one should worship the fourteen Yamas:
Yama, Dharmaraja, Mrityu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kala, Sarvabhutakshaya,
Audumbara, Dadhna, the two Nila and Parameshthi, Vrikodara, Chitra and Chitragupta — fourteen;
worshipping them with perfumes and other offerings, one should then offer libations with handfuls of water mixed with sesame, with darbha, three to each;
then one should give an arghya to the Sun in a copper vessel, O Narada, with water, red sandal, sesame, unbroken rice and barley:
Come, thousand-rayed Sun, mass of radiance, lord of the world; accept the arghya I give with devotion and have compassion on me.
Having given the arghya with this mantra, and fed fourteen brahmins, giving a good fee of silver, one should dismiss them and eat oneself.
Having performed the rite thus, O brahmin, by Dharmaraja's grace one enjoys pleasures, sons and wealth of this world, rare even for gods,
and at the end of the body, riding an excellent celestial car, reaches Vishnu's world.
One should install an excellent image of Vishnu, golden or silver, shining with four arms bearing conch, discus, mace and lotus,
clad in yellow, on a white, well-spread couch, O brahmin; then bathing it with the five nectars and with pure water with mantras,
one should prepare the offerings with the Purusha hymn, from the foot-water to the waving of lights, and then pray to Hari:
When you sleep, Lord of the world, this world sleeps; when you awaken, the whole world, moving and unmoving, awakens.
Having prayed thus before the god, the devoted man should take up, according to his capacity, the disciplines enjoined for the four months.
Then in the morning on the twelfth one should worship the one who lies on Shesha with the sixteen offerings, then feed brahmins,
please them with fees and eat in silence oneself. From then on, O best of brahmins, one should worship daily with perfumes and the like.
Having kept thus duly the vow of the god's sleeping, O brahmin, a mortal is endowed with enjoyment and liberation by Vishnu's grace.
